# Notes from the old orchard

The orchard is quieter in September. Most visitors come for the fruit, but I prefer the paths after the picking has finished. The grass is flattened beneath the trees, and the wooden ladders lean against the shed until someone finds time to put them away. A few apples remain too high to reach. They are a welcome meal for the birds.

This morning I followed the wall to the pond. The water was still, apart from a narrow trail behind a beetle. I sat on the bench and watched the reflections change as clouds crossed the sun. There was nothing urgent to do. The gate had been repaired, the tools were clean, and the sacks of fallen leaves could wait until tomorrow.

My neighbour joined me with a basket and a small notebook. She wanted to compare this year’s harvest with the figures her father had recorded. His entries were brief, sometimes no more than a date and a weight. Hers included weather, pests, and the names of people who had helped. Neither method told the whole story, but together they showed how the orchard had changed.

We talked about planting another pear tree near the south wall. The soil there drains well, although the corner is exposed to cold winds. We agreed to ask the gardener before choosing a variety. It would take years to know whether the decision had been a good one.

On the way home I stopped to close the gate. A dog was asleep on the other side, with one ear raised towards the sound of the latch. It opened its eyes, decided I was uninteresting, and went back to sleep.
